meta.description: Not Churchill. Quote Investigator traces this line to Keynes lore; the first strong match is Paul Samuelson in 1970, and no primary source pins it to anyone.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When the Facts Change, I Change My Mind. What Do You Do, Sir?'?
meta.ogDescription: Churchill did not say it. The famous wording is Keynes lore: the first strong match is Paul Samuelson, 1970. No primary source proves either man said it.

answer.label: Not Churchill — a paraphrase credited to John Maynard Keynes
answer.sourceLine: Winston Churchill is not the source. The earliest Churchill credit Quote Investigator ↗ can find is a 1999 item in the Florida Times-Union — and the wording there ends “What do you do, madam?”, not “sir”. The line belongs to Keynes lore instead, and even there no primary source exists: QI’s first strong match is Paul Samuelson on Meet the Press in 1970 saying “When events change, I change my mind. What do you do?”, and Samuelson credited Keynes only in 1978.

source.excerpt: Winston Churchill once said to a woman berating him for changing his position, “When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, madam?”
trail: 1924 — the near-miss. Keynes writes in The Nation and Athenaeum about the investor who “refuses to change his opinion merely because facts and circumstances have changed”. Same thought, none of the famous wording. Quote Investigator ↗

1970 — the first strong match. Paul Samuelson, on Meet the Press, defends revising his inflation estimates: “When events change, I change my mind. What do you do?” No attribution offered. He credits Keynes in the Wall Street Journal in 1978, and by 1983 is quoting it in The Economist as “When my information changes, I alter my conclusions. What do you do, sir?” Quote Investigator ↗

1999 — Churchill enters. The Florida Times-Union gives the line to Churchill, addressed to a woman: “What do you do, madam?” QI calls this connection tenuous, on both the lateness of the date and Churchill’s standing as a quotation magnet. Quote Investigator ↗

2011 — the search comes up empty. Wall Street Journal columnist Jason Zweig offers a cash bounty for an irrefutable primary source, betting he will never have to pay it out; economist Donald Moggridge of the University of Toronto answers him, “The simple answer…is there is no evidence.” Jason Zweig ↗
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest Churchill version Quote Investigator can locate — a newspaper anecdote, decades into the line’s life, with no source of its own. Note that it says “madam,” not “sir”: the “sir” ending comes from the Keynes branch of the story, where Samuelson’s 1983 version reads “When my information changes, I alter my conclusions. What do you do, sir?”

source.rightsNote: No work by Churchill or by Keynes has ever been shown to contain this sentence, so there is no first publication whose date could fix a copyright status — we assert none. Its nearest documented ancestor is a 1970 broadcast remark by Paul Samuelson, and Churchill’s own line on consistency, quoted on this page, comes from an essay collected in Thoughts and Adventures (1932); neither is treated here as public domain.

author.name: John Maynard Keynes
author.kicker: The man the line is usually pinned on
author.heading: So whose line is it?
author.metaLine: 1883–1946 · English economist, called the father of macroeconomics
author.bio: John Maynard Keynes was the English economist whose The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) reshaped how governments think about slumps, spending and unemployment. He was a famous changer-of-position — on the gold standard, on public works, on his own forecasts — which is exactly why a snappy defence of changing your mind attached itself to his name so easily. But no letter, article, broadcast or book of his has ever been produced containing this sentence, and his biographer Lord Robert Skidelsky told the investment writer William Bernstein in 2003 that this line and “the market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent” were both apocryphal.

copyAttribution: Not Winston Churchill. "When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?" is usually credited to John Maynard Keynes, but no primary source has ever been produced for either man. Quote Investigator's first strong match is Paul Samuelson on Meet the Press, 20 December 1970 — "When events change, I change my mind. What do you do?" — and Samuelson credited Keynes only in 1978. The earliest Churchill credit QI records is a Florida Times-Union item of 18 September 1999, and it says "madam," not "sir." Keynes's biographer Lord Robert Skidelsky told the investment writer William Bernstein in 2003 that this line and "the market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent" were both apocryphal.

misattribution.heading: A double misattribution
misattribution.intro: Two names get this line, and neither can be shown to have said it. Churchill is the newer and weaker claim; Keynes is the older and more plausible one, but “more plausible” is not the same as sourced.

items.why: The earliest Churchill credit Quote Investigator ↗ found is a 1999 Florida Times-Union item: “Winston Churchill once said to a woman berating him for changing his position, ‘When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, madam?’” QI’s verdict is that the connection is “tenuous because the attribution occurred at such a late date and because Churchill’s name attracts spurious ascriptions.”

Wikiquote ↗ lists it only under “Attributed”, and files the popular form as a paraphrase of the version Paul Samuelson reported in The Economist in 1983: “When my information changes, I alter my conclusions. What do you do, sir?” Separately, Keynes’s biographer Lord Robert Skidelsky told the investment writer William Bernstein by e-mail in 2003 that this line and “the market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent” were “both apocryphal” Jason Zweig ↗.

QI’s earliest strong match is Samuelson on Meet the Press on 20 December 1970, defending having revised his inflation estimates between textbook editions: “When events change, I change my mind. What do you do?” He gave no attribution then; he credited Keynes in the Wall Street Journal in 1978. Quote Investigator ↗

Romney credited a version of the line to Churchill on the campaign trail, and the International Churchill Society ↗ replied that he had confused Churchill with Keynes — while allowing that the sentiment was one Churchill genuinely held.

misattribution.truthLine: No primary source has ever been produced for this sentence — not from Churchill, not from Keynes. The earliest strong match Quote Investigator ↗ documents is Paul Samuelson in 1970, and even Samuelson only attached Keynes’s name to it eight years afterwards.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Churchill
lead: Churchill is the internet’s highest-gravity quotation magnet: a line that sounds like a witty man demolishing a heckler drifts toward him whether or not he was in the room. This one had an extra pull, because Churchill really did spend a fifty-year career being accused of inconsistency — he crossed the floor of the Commons twice — and he really did have an answer ready. It just wasn’t this one.

The irony, as the International Churchill Society pointed out when Mitt Romney credited a version of the line to Churchill in 2011, is that Churchill’s genuine sentence on the subject is better than the one people borrow for him. It appears in his essay “Consistency in Politics,” collected in Thoughts and Adventures, and you can read it in full at the Internet Archive ↗.
context.detailsSummary: What Churchill actually wrote about changing your mind
detailsBody: In “Consistency in Politics,” Churchill argues that a statesman’s arguments in two different situations may look “contradictory in spirit and opposite in direction” while his object stays the same: “We cannot call this inconsistency. In fact it may be claimed to be the truest consistency.” Then comes the pull-quote above.

The International Churchill Society dates the article to 1927, in Nash’s Pall Mall, and notes it was reprinted in Thoughts and Adventures. That is the Churchill line on this subject — documented, in his own book, and nothing like the sentence the internet hands him.
context.pull: The only way a man can remain consistent amid changing circumstances is to change with them while preserving the same dominating purpose.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's chronology: Keynes's 1924 Nation and Athenaeum passage; Paul Samuelson's 1970 Meet the Press remark 'When events change, I change my mind. What do you do?' as the first strong match; Samuelson crediting Keynes in the Wall Street Journal in 1978 and in The Economist in 1983; the 1999 Florida Times-Union Churchill attribution ending 'What do you do, madam?'; Skidelsky's 2003 'both apocryphal' e-mail; and the conclusion that the Churchill connection is tenuous.

Wikiquote lists 'When my information changes, I alter my conclusions. What do you do, sir?' under its Attributed section for Keynes, citing Samuelson in The Economist (June 1983), and notes it 'has also been paraphrased as "When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?"'

Jason Zweig reports that no primary source can be produced for the quotation, offered a cash bounty ($10 for one source, $20 for both), cites Skidelsky's 2003 'both apocryphal' assessment, and quotes Donald Moggridge of the University of Toronto: 'The simple answer...is there is no evidence.'

The International Churchill Society states that Mitt Romney confused Churchill with Keynes over this line, and quotes Churchill's genuine sentence 'The only way a man can remain consistent amid changing circumstances is to change with them while preserving the same dominating purpose', dating the article 'Consistency in Politics' to 1927 in Nash's Pall Mall, reprinted in Thoughts and Adventures.

The full text of Churchill's essay 'Consistency in Politics' contains the sentence 'The only way a man can remain consistent amid changing circumstances is to change with them while preserving the same dominating purpose', preceded by 'We cannot call this inconsistency. In fact it may be claimed to be the truest consistency.'
Wikiquote's Winston Churchill page does not list 'When the facts change, I change my mind' in any section (sourced, attributed, disputed or misattributed).

Keynes was born 5 June 1883 and died 21 April 1946; he was an English economist called the 'father of macroeconomics', whose magnum opus was The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936).
